title: Cabernet Sauvignon around the world
subtitle: The grape that travelled furthest
objectives: Describe Cabernet in Bordeaux's Left Bank

steps.title: The Left Bank
steps.body: Cabernet Sauvignon is a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, born in Bordeaux in the 17th century. On the gravel soils of the Médoc, which drain well and store heat, it leads the blend in wines like Pauillac and Margaux. The style: blackcurrant, cedar, high tannin and acidity, built to age.

steps.title: Late ripening
steps.body: Cabernet buds and ripens late. In cool years it can keep a green pepper note, from pyrazines that only break down with full ripeness. That's why it needs warm, well-drained sites. Warm regions like Napa Valley give riper blackcurrant, softer tannins and 14.5% alcohol or more.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon thrive on the gravel of the Médoc?
options: Gravel drains and stores heat, helping a late ripener
steps.explanation: Gravel warms the roots and drains water, both helping a late-ripening grape in a moderate climate.

steps.title: Napa, Chile and Australia
steps.body: Napa Valley made Cabernet famous in the New World after the Judgment of Paris in 1976. Chile's Maipo gives ripe blackcurrant with a minty note. Australia's Coonawarra, on red terra rossa soil, gives eucalyptus and mint; Margaret River gives an elegant, Bordeaux-like style.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet character.
steps.explanation: Cabernet keeps its blackcurrant core while place changes the rest.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet leads the blends of Bordeaux's gravelly Left Bank
As a late ripener it needs warmth, or it tastes green
Napa, Maipo, Coonawarra and Margaret River each give a distinct style
